item.description: Not surprising at all. I was paying too much attention to stressful and negative-tone videos, and I found myself thinking/feeling more negative. I didn’t like it, so I changed my algorithm by skipping that stuff. Much better! Laura Walsh Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Scientists revive decades-old approach to target cancer-linked genes using synthetic DNA
item.description: Researchers have developed a new approach that uses synthetic DNA molecules to target cancer-linked genes directly, opening new possibilities for future treatments, diagnostics and biological research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Double mutualist' birds are key to mistletoe reproduction
item.description: Some bird species act as "double mutualists" for a common mistletoe, both pollinating its flowers and dispersing its seeds. These double mutualists play an effective role in mistletoe reproduction. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are Counter-Strike players better at decision-making? Study reveals faster brain processing in expert gamers
item.description: Expert Counter-Strike players could make ideal candidates for fast-paced emergency service response jobs requiring split-second decision-making, according to a new University of Sheffield study aiming to debunk myths about video games. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tell this AI what you want a protein to do—and it designs one
item.description: In a short space of time, artificial intelligence has become a whiz at designing proteins, molecular machines that perform various functions such as speeding up reactions, producing fluorescent signals and breaking down plastic. But getting AI to design the specific protein you want usually requires the user to have a strong understanding of molecular structures and geometric constraints to guide the models correctly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI is changing what's in store for new hires and managers alike
item.description: AI is screening résumés, prompting some managers to hire fewer entry-level workers and leading others to expect beginners to tackle more advanced work, Northeastern University's AI & Society Survey found. The report is the latest in a series that opened with an analysis of how people across the political spectrum view AI training. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plants' immune memory hints at new crop breeding approach
item.description: A study published in Nature Communications, led by professor Jurriaan Ton and Dr. Adam Hannan Parker at the University of Sheffield, has identified mechanisms by which plants maintain and reset stress memory from past infections. This immune memory enables plants to defend themselves more effectively against harmful bacteria and mildews, which are increasingly threatening our crop and food production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unos científicos italianos viajaron a Etiopía a estudiar monos y volvieron con una inverosímil historia de amor entre un burro y un toro
item.description: En un pasto comunal de Debre Libanos, en las tierras altas de Etiopía, un burro llamado Patroclo busca a un toro llamado Achille en mitad del prado. Se le acerca y le toca con el hocico en el costado. Pasan cosas, aparecen terceros en discordia. Hay peleas, algún mordisco. Pero al final, juntos otra vez, el toro monta al asno y se queda lamiéndolo. Pero esa escena, grabada en vídeo con otras tantas, no era un hecho aislado. Lo que los investigadores italianos acaban de encontrar es una relación que desafía lo que sabemos sobre conducta animal : dos machos de familias distintas que, con vacas… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Javier Jiménez

item.title: A new way to navigate tough land and water use decisions
item.description: An open-source software tool to help find a sweet spot between competing environmental and development demands has been launched by researchers at the University of Queensland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Boat burial reveals leprosy strain in fifth-century Germany
item.description: Visigothic and Vandal forces marched into Italy and conquered Rome; the Huns spread fear and terror on their campaigns through Western Europe; the Franks expanded their domain southward—the fifth century was an era of profound, often violent upheavals in Europe, and at the same time one of great mobility. Researchers from the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Christian-Albrechts-University in Kiel and the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research (NIhK) have now identified a specific example of this mobility in the Fallward burial ground in what is now the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Red and green auroras may share electron-driven origins
item.description: With their mysterious glow and swirling veils of color, auroras enchant even experienced researchers. When a particularly intense solar storm reached Earth on the night of May 10, 2024, and relevant websites predicted auroras even for southern Lower Saxony, several researchers from the Technical University of Braunschweig, the Fraunhofer Institute for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST, the University of Göttingen, and the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research (MPS) took to the outdoors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Park users reveal 5 factors shaping acceptance of wildlife management
item.description: Should an area be fenced off, should animals be sterilized or relocated—or, as a last resort, selectively culled? As the long-running controversy over white-tailed deer in the Montreal suburb of Longueuil's Michel-Chartrand Park has shown, managing wildlife in peri-urban parks isn't just about the science. Emotions, trust and how decisions are communicated also play a role. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Astronaut and Earth
item.description: CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk is pictured during the Oct. 29, 2026, spacewalk. The International Space Station was soaring 267 miles above the South Atlantic Ocean at the time of this photograph. Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon installed a new roll-out solar array on the space station and performed some get-ahead work […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Canadian scientists find dark colours and stripes could make buildings safer for seabirds
item.description: A study conducted at a seabird colony in Canada found that darker colours and patterned surfaces could reduce bird collisions caused by artificial lighting at night. Researchers discovered that vertically striped sheets recorded 2.8 times fewer bird collisions than plain sheets, while black sheets performed better than white ones. The findings could help make coastal buildings, ships and offshore facilities safer for seabirds. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: An asteroid's shape influences where a nuclear blast must be aimed to deflect it
item.description: If a dangerous asteroid were headed toward Earth, one defense could be a nuclear detonation to blast one side with X-rays and nudge it off course. But new simulations suggest that for a lumpy, irregular asteroid, exactly where those X-rays hit could make a huge difference. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New survey measures make double consciousness testable in studies of Black Americans
item.description: W.E.B. Du Bois' standing as a distinguished social scientist, with a distinguished body of work, has been subjected to the same marginalizing forces he examined in his pioneering scholarship on race, culture and Black social thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La carrera espacial privada tiene cada vez más “juguetes”: pronto tendrá también un telescopio en el espacio
item.description: La carrera espacial ya no es solo cosa de las grandes agencias públicas, como la NASA o la ESA. Las compañías privadas están teniendo un papel cada vez más relevante, especialmente en lo que respecta al desarrollo de cohetes y satélites. Hasta ahora, uno de los pocos terrenos inexplorados para el sector privado era el de los telescopios espaciales. Sin embargo, si todo va bien, eso cambiará muy pronto con el lanzamiento de Lazuli, el telescopio desarrollado por Schmidt Sciences para estudiar los exoplanetas que otros no han podido analizar en profundidad. 23 colores. Lazuli dispondrá de un… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: A type of Arctic Ocean bacteria may be using acetone to turn carbon into food
item.description: A newly identified Arctic Ocean bacterium may have an unusual way of making the building blocks it needs to grow. Using acetone, a common chemical in seawater, the bacteria incorporate carbon dioxide (CO₂) into their metabolisms, allowing them to survive in waters where nutrients and usable organic matter are scarce. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research ties heat to mealybug feeding and pasture damage
item.description: High temperatures change how mealybugs feed, and that could help explain why some pasture mealybug infestations do far more damage than others, according to early findings from Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists step closer to the 'Zeptoverse' after 42-year particle search
item.description: Physicists have found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it is expected to occur only around once in every 10 billion "beauty" particles. The result, from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), follows a search spanning more than 40 years and brings physicists closer to exploring the "Zeptoverse"—an unexplored world that exists at distances of a billionth of a trillionth of a meter, or a "zeptometer," where new particles and forces of nature may be hiding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to reduce harmful sexual behavior and protect your kids and their peers
item.description: Recent media reports of alleged sexual assaults by teenage boys draw attention to an uncomfortable truth: Young people sometimes perpetrate harmful sexual behavior against their peers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: TB 26-10 Printed Circuit Board Assembly Chip Resistor Body Cracking
item.description: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov. Download PDF here Chip resistors are widely used in NASA projects, yet cases of alumina substrate cracking during environmental testing are rare. Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration, with fractures occurring across the short axis due […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Afforestation reshapes wildfire activity across temperate regions worldwide
item.description: Tree planting provides wood, biomass and climate benefits, but the location where those new forests are established matters. An international study by researchers in Spain, Chile and Finland shows that converting nonforested land into planted forests can increase wildfire activity, with contrasting outcomes across temperate regions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Forgotten flint tools reveal how Egypt's farmers organized work before the pharaohs
item.description: More than a century after they were excavated from beneath Cairo, almost 3,000 stone tools from Heliopolis show that specialized work was already reshaping village life before Egypt became a state. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST may have found where heavy black hole seeds formed
item.description: Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern universe are the result of a long, drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBHs can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Astronaut, STEM Creator Connect with Students for STEM Day
item.description: Students across the country will have the opportunity to connect directly with the International Space Station during a live, interactive in-flight call with NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Mark Rober STEM content creator and founder of ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. The event, hosted by NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement, celebrates National STEM Day by bringing real‑world science, […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: En 2009, unos científicos encontraron pulpos caminando con cocos por el fondo del mar. Cuando descubrieron para qué eran, quedaron atónitos
item.description: En 2009, unos científicos descubrieron algo extraordinario en las aguas de Indonesia: pequeños pulpos que recogían restos y cáscaras de coco y caminaban con ellas por el fondo marino, a veces durante hasta 20 metros. Aquella forma de desplazarse era tan incómoda que los animales quedaban expuestos a sus depredadores. Hasta que los investigadores descubrieron para qué transportaban los cocos. El hallazgo terminó convirtiéndose en una de las observaciones más sorprendentes sobre la inteligencia de los invertebrados. Una escena difícil de creer. Durante cerca de una década, los biólogos Julian… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: 'Evolution in the act': Forest lizards reveal rapid adaptation in a warming world
item.description: Yale research scientist Saúl Domínguez-Guerrero didn't set out to catch "evolution in the act" when he traveled to the Caribbean with a team of Yale researchers a few years ago. At the time, the team from the lab of evolutionary biologist Martha Muñoz planned to do fieldwork on Caribbean anoles, colorful, tree-dwelling lizards native to warmer regions of the Americas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Many local communities know how to communicate during disasters. Let's learn from them
item.description: It was a frightening time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beetle poop may have helped shape millions of years of yeast evolution
item.description: University at Buffalo scientists have found evidence that different species of yeast have shared genes originally acquired from an ancient virus—and the guts and droppings of beetles may have helped make it happen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why we give flowers to those in grief—or buy them for ourselves when we're sad
item.description: During his renowned excavations at the Shanidar Cave in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, American archaeologist Ralph Solecki located burial sites containing pollen and flower fragments from various species of wildflowers. He interpreted this as evidence that Neanderthals may have placed flowers around their dead at their burial sites around 60,000 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why are we so squeamish about eating hagfish?
item.description: When fishers are out working their boats, they are typically targeting a specific type of fish. However, other species often end up in their nets or trawls as well. This is known as "bycatch"—seafood for which the fishers receive no payment. Although it is illegal to discard bycatch back into the sea, it still happens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fingernail-sized chip untangles mixed light into clean beams
item.description: Stanford engineers and colleagues designed a chip that can take a muddled mixture of light from multiple lasers and output clean beams of light. It's the first time researchers have demonstrated a device that can take in mixed, or partially coherent, light and sort its photons into a clear set of separate beams. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La NASA publicó una imagen de la Antártida en la que aparece una “calavera sonriente”
item.description: La apariencia quedó expuesta tras una suba en las temperaturas, que derritieron parte de la nieve que cubría la zona Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Trial of live facial recognition technology to catch criminals is putting people's privacy to the test
item.description: WA Police are using live facial recognition technology to help identify and arrest criminals, with significant results. The trial is the first of its kind in Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A tiny shift exposes a cold brown dwarf masquerading as an early galaxy
item.description: A faint red object spotted by the James Webb Space Telescope originally appeared to offer a possible glimpse of the universe's first galaxies. But images taken about 3½ years apart revealed a giveaway: The object, nicknamed Capotauro, had moved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unpacking wheat's water use for drought research
item.description: Researchers at The University of Queensland have developed a way to quantify how wheat varieties capture and convert soil water. Dr. Raul Gimenez from the Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation said the technique could be used to identify drought-tolerant crops. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Brazil publishes first global ‘roadmap’ for phasing out fossil fuels
item.description: Cop30 host sets out steps to break link with coal, oil and gas as it aims to move focus from negotiating to implementing All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit. Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference , set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas. Continue… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Fiona Harvey Environment editor

item.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
item.description: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to autism's origins hidden in the placenta
item.description: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between inflammation during pregnancy, placental damage, and autism-like traits in male mice, while females appeared naturally protected. The discovery could help explain why autism is diagnosed more frequently in boys and reveal new opportunities for early intervention. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day
item.description: Eating an avocado and a cup of mango every day may provide surprising benefits for heart health, according to a new study involving adults with prediabetes. After just eight weeks, participants experienced significant improvements in blood vessel function and diastolic blood pressure, particularly among men. These benefits occurred without weight gain or changes in calorie intake, suggesting that the nutrient-rich combination could support cardiovascular health through a simple dietary adjustment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
item.description: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Qué es el "zeptoverso", el mundo más pequeño jamás detectado en la naturaleza, y por qué es clave para entender el universo
item.description: Investigadores de la Universidad de Cambridge detectaron señales procedentes de la escala más pequeña de la naturaleza jamás explorada. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
item.description: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
item.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 10 asteroid mysteries that Hera will explore
item.description: Video: 00:07:25 Hera, the European Space Agency’s first mission for planetary defence, arrives at its target body during November, with the goal of gathering precious data on the kinetic impact method of asteroid deflection – while also solving various scientific enigmas. The small-car-sized spacecraft is headed to the 151-m-diameter Dimorphos asteroid, which orbits in turn around its 780-m Didymos parent. Dimorphos is already historic as the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit changed by human action – when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it on 26 September 2022. DART’s… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Monarch butterflies get tiny trackers to help scientists follow their mysterious migration
item.description: As a child, Rebeca Quiñonez-Piñón wondered where monarch butterflies stop for a meal and a night's rest on their long migrations across North America. Now she and other scientists are attaching tiny tracking devices to hundreds of butterflies to find those critical stopover locations before they disappear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 1610, one astronomer challenged Galileo’s discovery; their books survived together for centuries
item.description: In 1610, the revolutionary work of Galileo Galilei, titled Sidereus Nuncius, brought to light the moons orbiting Jupiter, challenging the traditional view of astronomy. This groundbreaking revelation incited controversy, notably with Francesco Sizzi, who dismissed these lunar discoveries as mere optical deceptions. Recently, a rare edition of Galileo's masterpiece fetched an astonishing Rs 2.07 crore, underscoring the enduring impact of his innovations amidst the scientific skepticism of his era. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Comet PanSTARRs and […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
item.description: Super Typhoon In-fa developed an unusually large eye, and the remnants of Typhoon Champi transitioned into an extratropical storm that targeted Alaska. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China imports millions of donkey hides from Africa every year: New book traces the drivers and impact
item.description: The demand for donkey hides has grown exponentially over the past 15 years, driven mainly by demand from China. Lauren Johnston is a specialist on China trade with Africa. She has spent several years looking into the donkey trade, and has just published a book, "China, Africa and the Market for Donkeys." She answers questions about what she found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How political disagreement with our neighbors relates to whether we bother casting a ballot
item.description: In the 2025 federal election, Canadians voted at the highest rate since 1993. Explanations for high or low turnout usually focus on the national election campaign, including how close the race was and what seemed to be at stake. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: HomeownerPal ha comentado: A whole new world past Neptune? Somewhere Luke Skywalker is squinting at two suns going, 'Told you there was more out there.'
item.description: Pluto may no longer be the outer solar system’s most intriguing dwarf planet. A newly spotted object, provisionally named ED138, could soon join its... Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions
item.description: North Korea rejected U.S. allegations linking it to the Binance hack as blockchain researchers traced billions in stolen cryptocurrency across networks. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Learjet may have broken up before crashing in Florida, investigators say
item.description: The National Transportation Safety Board said ⁠on Monday a Learjet ⁠60 that crashed on Sunday ⁠in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board, may have broken up before hitting the ground at high speed. The private Bombardier-made jet had taken off from Austin, Texas, and ‌was headed to the Bahamas. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area where it went down. Nasa Administrator Jared Isaacman, posting on X, highlighted the harrowing... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Study dives into lesser-known climate impacts of global reforestation
item.description: Simon Fraser University researchers are zeroing in on how global forestation efforts impact our climate system beyond CO₂ removal in a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
item.description: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ceres' water ice can mask massive surface salt deposits
item.description: The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an "asteroid" since it resides in the main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceres accounts for between 25% and 30% of the belt's total mass. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Pluto may no longer be the outer solar system’s most intriguing dwarf planet. ... Ver más A whole new world past Neptune? Somewhere Luke Skywalker is squinting at two suns going, 'Told you there was more out there.' Ver más comentarios HomeownerPal Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Ditching the shame as a sex worker living with a disability
item.description: I have a genetic connective tissue disorder, which makes everyday activities difficult. In my unconventional body, I chose unconventional work — sex work. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Climate change is making the tropics hotter
item.description: A new study finds that tropical areas often thought to be safe from the effects of climate change are actually experiencing significant changes in rainfall and extreme temperature events. The paper, "Shifting climate in Caribbean tropical forests: Long-term trends at La Selva (Costa Rica) and El Verde (Puerto Rico)," is published in PLOS Climate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese writing developed square forms gradually, shaped by language, tools and tradition, analysis suggests
item.description: A new historical analysis challenges the received wisdom as to why Chinese characters developed their distinctive square shapes. The work, published in the International Journal of Arts and Technology, argues that their shape resulted from interacting linguistic, technological and cultural factors rather than a single cause. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
item.description: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Europe's Gen Z protesters unite over living costs, housing and employment uncertainty
item.description: Although French high schoolers may have taken the lead in the youth protests that have since spread to Belgium, Germany, Italy, Portugal and Spain, they acted like "a catalyst" for their shared concerns over their future, researchers say, pointing to higher living costs, unaffordable housing and the uncertainty of their employment prospects. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE 24

item.title: UK storm surges have far-flung, global climate connections
item.description: Where a storm surge strikes along a stretch of U.K. coastline is decided by global climate patterns in the Atlantic, Arctic and even further afield—according to new research led by Cambridge University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Queen's University Belfast students find Neptune's elusive Trojan asteroids
item.description: An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has made a discovery that has eluded astronomers for decades. Beginning in 1906, telescope observations revealed a population of asteroids leading and trailing Jupiter, which came to be known as the "Trojan" and "Greek" populations. Since then, astronomers have discovered similar "families" orbiting Saturn and Uranus, but not Neptune. Thanks to the Queen's-led team, the mystery of the missing Trojans has now been resolved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Swift telescope predicted to plummet back to Earth tomorrow
item.description: After plans to save it failed, NASA's Swift telescope is hurtling back to Earth. Here's how to track its descent. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Genelle Weule

item.title: When to move is key to mobile retail
item.description: In recent years, the principle behind the humble ice cream truck has been getting a high-tech makeover. Retailers are reinventing mobile stores—both people-piloted and self-driving—often selling perishable items such as baked goods or fresh meals. BPM Analytics projects sales from retail on wheels will grow to $30 billion worldwide by 2030. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Gas inside us could fight wound infections, moth study shows
item.description: A gas naturally produced by our own bodies could one day help treat skin and wound infections, potentially offering a new approach alongside conventional antibiotics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Improved snow model captures Northeast's winter thaws and runoff more accurately
item.description: Mountain snow in the Northeast is different. The region's milder, more humid mountain climate shapes winter conditions that are different from those of the western United States. Yet, snow models don't always capture those differences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Analysis of Inca mummies identifies the drugs used in their most important sacrificial ritual
item.description: Archaeologists have performed toxicological analysis on the mummified remains of people sacrificed at mountain shrines across the Inca Empire, revealing the psychoactive substances they consumed before their deaths. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese PhD students in clinical medicine can graduate without a thesis — more degrees to follow
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03480-7 Postgraduate students studying professional medicine degrees can qualify with a ‘practical achievement’. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03508-y Climate change is reshaping urban environments. Architect Carlo Ratti tells Nature that technology offers solutions, but citizens must get the final say. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: David Adam

item.title: This cholesterol drug promised to be a game-changer. Why did it flop in the clinic — and is there still hope?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03504-2 Physicians were excited about several therapies that slash levels of lipoprotein(a) — an important cardiovascular risk factor. One major trial failed to show a benefit, and now scientists are scrambling to work out what that means. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Biotech firms are meant to pay to use Earth’s genetic data. They’re not.
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03554-6 Global leaders at COP17 biodiversity summit complained that companies using public genetic data are not paying into a voluntary fund to protect nature. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: James Dinneen

item.title: Telltale furrows: What the Baltic Sea seafloor reveals about bottom trawling
item.description: To what extent does bottom trawling impact the seafloor of the Baltic Sea—and how quickly does it recover? Two new studies from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW) show that the marks on the seafloor provide a much clearer picture of the actual impact than vessel position data alone. Using high-resolution echo sounder measurements and AI, the researchers reveal previously insufficiently recorded impacts and also document surprisingly rapid changes of the seafloor condition. Furthermore, they found strong indications of fishing violations in a marine protected area… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stem cells in deep sleep may point to a secret reserve for lifelong blood renewal
item.description: Researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the HI-STEM Stem Cell Institute have discovered a group of particularly long-lived blood stem cells in mice. These cells remain in a dormant state for an exceptionally long time while retaining their ability to generate new blood cells. This newly discovered cell population may be responsible for sustaining blood regeneration and immune defense throughout a mouse's entire life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Qué se sabe de la dramática caída de un avión privado en Florida que dejó 9 muertos
item.description: Investigadores de la Junta Nacional de Seguridad en el Transporte de EE.UU. informaron de los primeros indicios en la trágica caída de un jet privado que cobró la vida de todos sus ocupantes. Fuente: BBC News Mundo.

item.title: How competing reproductive needs shaped the evolution of liverworts
item.description: Liverworts reproduce through a life cycle involving two distinct stages. First, sperm fertilize eggs in the presence of water, producing embryos that develop into spore-producing structures called sporophytes. These structures then produce spores that can disperse and grow into new liverwort plants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Arctic plant roots may play key role in climate change
item.description: A new review involving researchers at Umeå University has revealed the critical role that plant roots play in shaping how Arctic tundra ecosystems respond to climate change. The paper, recently published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, highlights how processes occurring beneath the soil surface could help scientists better understand how one of the fastest-changing ecosystems on Earth will influence the future climate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plants may experience 'optical illusions' that affect their direction of growth
item.description: A new study from Tel Aviv University reveals how plants, despite having neither a brain nor a nervous system, integrate light coming from multiple directions to determine where to grow. The researchers show how this process emerges from local sensing across the stem, without the need for centralized information processing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea mussels trade tidal rhythms for a 24-hour cycle in the lab
item.description: Hydrothermal vents lie in perpetual darkness in the depths of the ocean, yet the cells of the vent mussel Bathymodiolus azoricus, which lives 1,700 meters (5,600 feet) below the surface, follow a 24-hour rhythm in the laboratory. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: To restore attention, reach out to nature
item.description: The world is a far louder and more distracting place than when humans first evolved. But there's increasing evidence that experiencing nature can help restore attention lost to modern distractions, known as "directed attention fatigue." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Impact of deep-sea mining on seafloor ecosystem still evident 44 years later
item.description: Little is known about the long-term effects of deep-sea mining on the organic matter that supports life on the seafloor. However, as interest in mining the deep sea for rare metals grows, there is concern that disturbing the seabed could affect the ecosystems of the deep ocean. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Exactly solvable model reveals how trapped light can create magnetic order in one-dimensional spin chains
item.description: A research team wanted to better understand how the forces between particles inside a material change. They discovered that by confining one-dimensional classical spin chains inside a mirror box cavity with light, they could force these magnetic particles to organize and undergo a phase transition. Their work provides the simplest exactly solvable examples showing that light can create new phase transitions with materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European flounder can complete whole life cycle in freshwater
item.description: Most flounders sampled in Lake Pulmanki in northern Finland had spent their entire lives in freshwater. The study provides the first evidence of the species living entirely in freshwater. The work is published in Evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
item.description: Article URL: https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2026-10-29-slac-researchers-find-proof-altermagnetism-new-magnetic-phase Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50344224 Points: 29 # Comments: 3 Fuente: Hacker News - Portada.

item.title: Industrialization reshapes gut microbes, from bacterial communities to their DNA, studies find
item.description: The totality of bacteria, viruses and fungi that exist in and on a multicellular organism forms its natural microbiome. The interactions between the body and these microorganisms significantly influence the host organism's functions and health. Among other things, researchers have shown that the microbiome plays an important role in defense against pathogens. On the other hand, they suspect that imbalances in the microbiome's composition are linked to the development of so-called environmental diseases, such as chronic inflammation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
item.description: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sumer Loggins

item.title: Are we overfertilizing our fields? Researchers challenge conventional soil testing
item.description: A new study led by Dr. Shikma Zaarur of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, in collaboration with Dr. Ran Erel of the Agricultural Research Organization–Volcani Institute, reveals that agricultural soils may contain a substantial unaccounted-for reservoir of potassium, an essential nutrient for plant growth, that is largely overlooked by conventional soil testing methods. The findings could pave the way for more precise fertilizer recommendations, potentially reducing unnecessary fertilizer use while supporting sustainable agricultural production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular dinitrogen anions pave the way for low-temperature ammonia synthesis
item.description: While ammonia (NH₃) is best known for its role in fertilizer production, it is attracting attention as a carbon-free hydrogen carrier, potentially offering a practical way to store and transport clean fuel. Despite this promise, NH₃ synthesis still depends on high-temperature, high-pressure processes that are difficult to scale up sustainably. The reason behind this is the extremely strong bond between nitrogen atoms in nitrogen gas (N₂), which requires a lot of energy to break. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: According to science, you may be more likely to gain respect and status by helping others
item.description: Human intelligence is still a bit of an enigma. Researchers have some ideas about why advanced intelligence evolved in humans, but they have not come to a conclusive answer. One prominent idea is that intelligence serves a social function. In their new study, a group of researchers led by Jonathan Egeland reports additional evidence supporting this idea. According to their research, published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior, greater intelligence seems to garner more respect, but only when it's applied to tasks that help others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region
item.description: Scientists studying the neurology of tame foxes identified changes in a part of the brain that has previously been associated with aggression, according to a new paper that compared the brains of domesticated, aggressive and wild foxes. The changes occurred in an area at the base of the brain called the ventromedial hypothalamus, which is known to drive aggression, control decisions related to energy use and play an important role in maternal instincts and social behaviors in mice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov. Download the PDF version An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform. When the complete force and response are measured accurately, crest ripples and separated contacts remain known inputs. Force shape changes excitation, but does not inherently invalidate the record. item.title: Q&A: Is faith feminine? Why US churches have men in pulpits, women in pews
item.description: Working as a Christian minister years ago, Landon Schnabel noticed a paradox common to many U.S. churches: Men filled leadership roles, implying that religion is masculine and patriarchal, but many more women participated in services, Bible study and other activities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new way to make better use of ruthenium in single-atom catalysts
item.description: Ruthenium (Ru) is a valuable metal used in catalysts to speed up chemical reactions in many industrial processes. It can help improve efficiency and reduce the energy needed for chemical production. However, because it is rare and expensive, scientists are looking for ways to make better use of it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrashort laser pulses can slice lab-grown diamond along useful crystal plane
item.description: More than just a precious gemstone for jewelry, diamond has properties that make it attractive for several next-generation, high-performance technologies. Its high thermal conductivity can help move heat away from semiconductor devices, while its wide bandgap is promising for high-power electronics. Moreover, its transparency in the visible light range makes diamond useful for demanding optical applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: RNA-protein interactions could lead to new coronavirus drug targets
item.description: A study co-led by a University of California, Riverside, biomedical scientist has identified new targets for coronavirus antiviral drugs, including treatments that may be less vulnerable to the rapid evolution of these viruses. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Historical records reveal the bitter truth about 17th-century Transylvania's climate
item.description: For roughly five centuries from about 1300, Europe experienced periods of unusually cold weather and extreme conditions collectively known as the Little Ice Age. Transylvania, a historical region in modern-day Romania, was also affected, but information about just how severe things were had been scattered in old town records, church logs, travelogs and administrative and monastic diaries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
item.description: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue. But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago… Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ian Sample Science editor

item.title: Fighting accent bias is everyone's job, not just accented speakers'
item.description: People who speak with an accent know it can lead to discrimination. It can cost them in job interviews, at work and in everyday exchanges. But what they usually have to go on is anecdote: their own experiences and those of people they know. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stars make oxygen for small galaxies, but they lose most of it
item.description: Scientists examining data collected by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope have found that dozens of small galaxies contain far less oxygen than their stars are estimated to have produced. The researchers, including a Rutgers astrophysicist, studied 37 dwarf galaxies, which are much smaller than the Milky Way and considered to be nearby, within 22 million light-years of Earth. The results were published in The Astrophysical Journal. Fuente: Phys.org.
